children.author: mikestylz
children.text:
> Should we assume that all software is more compromised than the kernel?

Absolutely, the front door has always been unlocked. We were previously protected by the economics of exploit detection favoring the developers, but now we have entered a new world.

The issues arise almost everywhere we look. It's frustrating because the user experience in edge systems has barely changed in the last fifteen years. We could have rode the advances in semiconductor manufacturing to embed more layers of protection such as CHERI while slightly slowing down the rate of performance improvements. Instead we have only marginally upgraded security and largely added features which the users scarcely notice.

I am hopeful about the long term prospects of formal verification, but having humans reviewing the proof statements and confirming they match our desired properties will take many years. Meanwhile, AI assisted hacking is an urgent issue. So we will have to delegate implementation, proof specification, and proof development to the AIs in the short term. Maybe that goes well, but who knows. Interesting times.

You're painting a picture that code written with love is perfectly safe. It's not.

Yes, openbsd has not had a torrent of bugs found, but I would say that the vastly bigger reasons for that are: 1) orders of magnitude people care about burning tokens and money to find the bugs in an OS almost nobody uses, and 2) it's simply much smaller. Can't have Bluetooth bugs if you don't have a Bluetooth stack.

I've pointed LLMs at obsd stuff, and even the simplest code, e.g. cat & find, had bugs and buffer overflows.

OpenBSD also has a poor patch tracking system, since they're still on CVS. A patch has an extremely good chance of just falling through the cracks. Security or not.

So no. Nobody can write safe C. Not hobbyists, and not "those evil corporations".

Because the large corporations that fund Linux development and use Linux value speed over security.

Speed requires a lot of code in the kernel, where that code can run fast.

There are kernels that do not have a thousand privilege escalation exploits. These kernels are smaller and much easier to check for bugs. But those kernels are significantly slower.

For many use cases, slower is not a problem. But for the large corporations who fund a lot of Linux development and use Linux in large data centers, every 1% slower can literally be millions of dollars worth of additional servers that are required.

OpenBSD shows that you can have a Unix security model without a thousand privilege escalation exploits. But OpenBSD is like 10% slower. So corporations won't use it because it would cost millions of dollars more per year and some of their software requires access that OpenBSD does not grant precisely because that access leads to security exploits (i.e. io_uring, eBPF etc. etc.)

You could also use like seL4, but that's slow too

So that's why. It's a business tradeoff between cost of servers vs cost of getting hacked, and cost of servers wins.

Not really, no. If you're running an application server, then your entire app can get compromised if there's a security exploit in any of your app code, your web server, your kernel, your hypervisor.

Defense in depth says that simply compromising your application code shouldn't provide access to the physical hardware you're running on, and that's hopefully the case, but it doesn't mean your app is not hacked. It just hopefully means that a hack on your app code doesn't automatically give the attacker access to your entire company.

> There are just too many layers underneath the good ol' web application to claim that AI won't succeed.

I think you got it backwards. For your AI to succeed, it needs to poke a hole on all layers, not one in many layers. If an attacker pokes a hole in n-1 layers but the 1 layer remains untouched, the system's integrity is preserved.

Why do you think defense in depth is a basic concept?

And then your language has a gaping hole (PHP or NodeJS), or the box you're running on has a gaping hole (Linux), or the PaaS you use has a gaping hole (Railway). There are just too many layers underneath the good ol' web application to claim that AI won't succeed.

Honestly, at this point the best we have is to hope the whitehat AI scanning for issues is stronger than the blackhat AI.

I don't think this is true in general. If you deploy a good ole web application with sufficiently locked down inputs and thorough input validation, the AI will not succeed. children.text:
Cybersecurity operates under the "not enough bears" theory of security. There are a million people in a valley and a male and female bear. You do not need to outrun the bears, you just need to outrun the two slowest people. Next year there are more bears, but you still only need to outrun a few people. Then, one day, there are a million bears and they eat you all. But that day has not happened yet.

To explain more seriously, almost all visible cyberattacks are carried out by profit-motivated criminals. This has a very clear cost-benefit analysis; your revenue is hacking organizations and extorting them for available money, and your costs are developing and deploying attacks. The ROI is outrageously good easily being on the order of 10x to 100x. If it is so easy and so profitable why do not they just hack all of the millions of organizations on the planet with millions of dollars of available cash for trillions of dollars of revenue? Sure, all they have to do is create a trillion dollar revenue commercial organization bootstrapping themselves with no outside investors, loans, or access to financial resources or the financial system.

I mean, it took Mark Zuckerberg 20 years and a metric ton of VC investment and public investment to make 200 billion dollars in revenue. So what kind of loser can not make a commercial organization 5x larger with a trillion dollars in revenue in less time with no outside investors? Are they even trying? Just make more revenue than any other commercial organization in the entire world and extract that money in a freely usable form, how hard can that be?

They are not there yet, but they are trying. If you look at cybercrime reports you see something like 3x-10x growth year over year. Ransomware reports from a few years ago were showing a 3x year over year growth in number of attacks and simultaneously a 3x year over year growth in ransom amount with the averages being on the order of 100,000 dollars. Chump change for any serious organization, but give that a few years of 3x and that starts to look like real money. However, as it becomes real money it becomes harder and harder to launder it into a usable form. Sure, you could hit someone for 30 million dollars, but how are you going to get that into your bank account? Cryptocurrency helps some, but even there the big money tries to steer away from large overt crime. Maybe you could launder a few tens of billions a year that way, but that is still a far cry from the trillions for everything everywhere.

And of course even assuming you can scale your organization 10x year over year it still takes a decade of sustained growth, scaling your hiring and organization across 9 orders of magnitude, to get to billions per year. A literal decade even if you were growing at a outrageous pace for a outrageous amount of time just to reach a fraction of the total addressable market. A decade of that and you are still nowhere near blowing up all the power plants. Give it time, we need a lot of bears to get there.

Doesn’t this imply a software design issue where it is just written in a way to have these security bugs and patching them 1 by 1 is not what should be done but the whole design should change which can eliminate full classes of security bugs without any particular patches being necessary?

children.text:
Your argument is literal red herring. Postgres is a different project with different codebase and vastly different-sized security team.

Why not look at something like SQLite instead and conclude that things are great?

> The community is already doing a great job at finding and patching the actual vulns without the attention-desperate big labs.

It is however reasonable to assume that a lot of bugs that are being found by the community these days were found thanks to those people using AI to aid them.

See for example what a PostgreSQL developer is saying:

> All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL’s code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That’s always been true, and it hasn’t stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs. […]

> […]

> […] a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very, very busy fixing them […]

http://rhaas.blogspot.com/2026/10/postgres-19-is-late-and-it...

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50312408

It feels like this comment section has either gotten collective amnesia or didn't watch Greg KH's video on previous dump and grossly exaggerated claims from Anthropic [0].

From his talk, AIs can't reliably deduplicate or count vulnerabilities, dash for easy and meaningless escape hatches like malicious filesystems, and report the same things as found by everyone else. Indeed, this post literally says: "Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed."

A few ready takeaways: this is just hype. The community is already doing a great job at finding and patching the actual vulns without the attention-desperate big labs. And no, you absolutely do not need to pay them a million dollars each year for the privilege.

This behavior is the same thing that OpenAI has been doing to math -- produce tons of slop that are useless to humans. But this time, we don't even get to see how bad it is because they need to hide it to protect our precious little minds. We have got to be afraid though, very afraid.

Our field really needs someone like Terry Tao to unambiguously stand up to this behavior and say that they are not welcome to take such dumps on everyone.

[0]: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NnV_cWeoo5Q
